title: Your Seller Summary May Be Borrowing a Product's Rating
author: vexaloom-labs
summary: Your agent can read the right rating and still rate the wrong thing. You wire a seller check into your weekend agent project. The summary sounds reassuring, but its evidence includes the rating of something the shop sells. Excellent kettle. Unanswered question about the shop. Lab note 093: can we keep product reputation out of a seller summary before the model sees it? The records below are synthetic, and public profile data supports a check rather than completing a vetting decision. Why does seller mode mix reputation? Seller mode emits catalog products by default, so name and rating can describe different entities in the same dataset. The dataset holds four record types, distinguished by recordType . Flattening their shared fields removes the distinction your agent needs. Example synthetic records make the collision visible without making claims about a real seller: example_rows = [ { "recordType" : "seller" , "sellerId" : "123456" , "name" : "Example storefront" , "rating" : 4.2 , "url" : "https://www.ozon.ru/seller/123456/" , "scrapedAt" : "2026-10-01T12:00:00Z" , } , { "recordType" : "product" , "name" : "Example kettle" , "rating" : 5.0 , } , ] Both ratings are valid properties of their respective records. A generic “summarize these names and ratings” instruction has already discarded the subject of each score. There's another catch: maxItems counts emitted records, including the profile. With maxItems: 20 , the result can include the seller row plus up to 19 catalog products. That makes catalog rows a tempting source of extra evidence. They're also evidence about a different thing. Put the MCP connection behind the wrapper The useful boundary is between retrieval and interpretation: agent supplies seller ID | v wrapper pins seller-only input | v Actor returns records | v type + identity checks -> explicit seller fields -> agent This MCP client configuration exposes the Actor to a private execution host. The server process inherits APIFY_TOKEN from its environment. { "mcpServers" : { "seller-source" : { "command" : "npx" , "args" : [ "-y" , "@apify/actors-mcp-server" , "--actors" , "vexaloom-labs/ozon-ru-product-pricing-ratings-and-seller-scraper" ] } } } That connection alone doesn't enforce a seller-only contract. It exposes the Actor's input surface. Your summarizing agent should receive a narrower MCP tool, check_seller , whose handler applies the policy below. Keep the raw Actor tool available to the execution host rather than registering it alongside the wrapper for that agent. Otherwise, the agent can simply choose the broader tool. We'd rather remove that decision. Let the agent choose the target For this wrapper, we'd accept a numeric seller ID. The Actor also accepts storefront URLs and slugs, but a numeric target gives this small implementation a direct identity comparison. That restriction is deliberate. Supporting aliases requires an explicit resolution step, not a hopeful comparison between a storefront name and a URL. Setting Wrapper policy Reason sellerUrls Build from the agent's single seller ID Keeps the request tied to an explicit target mode Pin to "seller" Prevents a seller check from becoming a product lookup includeSellerProducts Pin to false Removes the catalog branch at retrieval maxItems Pin to 1 Bounds emitted records for this narrow task storefront Pin to "ru" Makes the selected market part of the tool contract Leave product filters outside this tool. Filtering inventory by price or product rating doesn't establish anything about the seller's profile rating. If you later need assortment analysis, give it a separate tool with a separate response shape. The names should tell the agent which question each tool can answer. Preserve the subject when you serialize Disabling catalog emission is the input fix. Checking the returned records is the output fix. The following projection rejects mixed types, ambiguous cardinality, and an identity mismatch before serialization. Its renamed keys belong to our wrapper, not to the Actor. seller_fields = { "recordType" : "recordType" , "sellerId" : "sellerId" , "name" : "seller_name" , "rating" : "seller_profile_rating" , "reviewsCount" : "seller_profile_reviews_count" , "ordersCount" : "seller_orders_count" , "legalName" : "seller_legal_name" , "registrationNumber" : "seller_registration_number" , "url" : "url" , "scrapedAt" : "scrapedAt" , } def project_seller ( rows , expected_seller_id ) : if any ( row . get ( "recordType" ) != "seller" for row in rows ) : raise ValueError ( "Non-seller record in seller-check response" ) if len ( rows ) != 1 : raise ValueError ( "Expected exactly one seller profile" ) seller_row , = rows if str ( seller_row . get ( "sellerId" , "" ) ) != expected_seller_id : raise ValueError ( "Seller identity is missing or mismatched" ) if not seller_row . get ( "url" ) or not seller_row . get ( "scrapedAt" ) : raise ValueError ( "Seller evidence lacks source or observation time" ) return { alias : seller_row [ source ] for source , alias in seller_fields . items ( ) if source in seller_row } We don't take the first row and declare it the requested entity. Position in a dataset isn't identity. Missing optional fields stay missing. The Actor omits empty values, so an absent rating mustn't become a neutral score, and an absent registration number mustn't become evidence that registration doesn't exist. Here's the handler logic to bind to your agent-facing MCP tool. It uses the Python client for execution; MCP registration remains specific to your host. import os from apify_client import ApifyClient client = ApifyClient ( os . environ [ "APIFY_TOKEN" ] ) def check_seller ( seller_id : str ) : if ( not isinstance ( seller_id , str ) or not seller_id . isascii ( ) or not seller_id . isdecimal ( ) ) : raise ValueError ( "Supply one numeric seller ID as a string" ) run_input = { "mode" : "seller" , "sellerUrls" : [ seller_id ] , "includeSellerProducts" : False , "maxItems" : 1 , "storefront" : "ru" , } run = client . actor ( "vexaloom-labs/ozon-ru-product-pricing-ratings-and-seller-scraper" ) . call ( run_input = run_input ) if run [ "status" ] != "SUCCEEDED" : raise RuntimeError ( f "Seller collection ended with {run['status']}" ) items = client . dataset ( run [ "defaultDatasetId" ] ) . list_items ( ) . items return project_seller ( items , seller_id ) The function accepts no list and offers no switch for adding inventory. The agent gets a target choice, not a collection-policy editor. Budget the evidence after projection Token trimming before entity selection can preserve the wrong evidence very efficiently. Start with the seller projection, serialize it, then measure the exact text you intend to send. Don't truncate serialized JSON halfway through a source URL to meet a budget. This cell checks rejection of the synthetic mixture and measures the accepted seller context: import json import tiktoken try : project_seller ( example_rows , "123456" ) except ValueError : pass else : raise AssertionError ( "Mixed records must be rejected" ) seller_context = project_seller ( [ row for row in example_rows if row . get ( "recordType" ) == "seller" ] , "123456" , ) context_text = json . dumps ( seller_context , ensure_ascii = False , separators = ( "," , ":" ) ) encoding = tiktoken . get_encoding ( "cl100k_base" ) context_tokens = len ( encoding . encode ( context_text ) ) context_tokens measures this encoding's token count, not a universal count for every model. For a larger response, remove optional evidence deliberately and measure again. Preserve identity, source, and observation time together: a compact rating without its subject is how this annoyance started. What still breaks the check A successful run status isn't proof of complete collection. Partial failures can leave valid rows available, and mirror availability can affect coverage. The wrapper therefore treats an empty response as an error, not as a seller with nothing concerning to report. It also refuses unrelated records instead of feeding them to the model as consolation data. The worked example uses Ozon.ru Product Pricing, Ratings & Seller Scraper . Legal identifiers help with entity matching, but their presence doesn't establish that a prospective business relationship is safe. Cross-check the legal entity through an appropriate independent source before making that decision. Likewise, a product's favorable reviews can support a product assessment. They don't become seller-profile evidence merely because the product appears in that seller's catalog. Give the agent a smaller promise Our verdict: make the tool return seller evidence, then ask the agent to explain it. A prompt that says “don't confuse the ratings” still leaves the confusion available. A typed projection removes the competing score and names the remaining score's subject. Keep the agent's instruction equally narrow: describe the seller profile, identify missing evidence, and preserve the source and observation time. Don't turn the profile rating into a blanket approval. That's a useful weekend-sized fix. The model can spend its attention on the evidence instead of deciding whose reputation it has been handed. Reproduce the boundary check Run the synthetic cells to check that mixed records are rejected and inspect context_tokens . Bind check_seller as your MCP handler, exposing only its string argument. Set APIFY_TOKEN in the execution environment and substitute your intended seller ID. Submit the following Actor input through the handler's pinned path. Example input, using a placeholder seller ID that you should replace: { "mode" : "seller" , "sellerUrls" : [ "123456" ] , "includeSellerProducts" : false , "maxItems" : 1 , "storefront" : "ru" }

title: ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10 (Fix)
author: Yunus Emre Güzel
summary: Your script runs, then Python stops with this: ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '3.50' You gave int() a string that doesn't look like a whole number. The end of the message shows the exact text Python choked on, in quotes. So the error already tells you what's wrong. Below are the six inputs that cause it most often, and how to fix each one. I ran every example on Python 3.11, 3.12 and 3.14. All three print the same message. What the Error Means int(text) turns a string like "42" into the number 42. It takes an optional sign and digits. It also ignores spaces and a newline at either end, so int(" 42\n") works. Anything else breaks it: a decimal point, a comma, a letter, an empty string. Python raises a ValueError for those. Why not a TypeError ? Because a string is the right type. This particular value just isn't usable. The real cause is where the string came from. Text from input() , a file line, a CSV cell, a web form or an API is always text. And text can hold anything. How to Find the Cause Fast Look at the quoted text at the end of the message. That's the string that failed. If it might hide odd characters, print it with repr() : print ( repr ( text ) ) Then compare what you see with the six cases below. The Six Causes 1. An Empty String text = "" # for example, the user just pressed Enter number = int ( text ) # ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '' The message ends in : '' , with nothing between the quotes. You'll see it when someone hits Enter at an input() prompt. You'll also see it with an empty CSV cell, or when a split line leaves an empty piece. Catch the error, then decide what an empty value should mean: text = "" try : number = int ( text ) except ValueError : number = 0 # or ask again print ( number ) 2. A Decimal Number price = "3.50" cents = int ( price ) # ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '3.50' Odd, but true: int() happily takes the float 3.5 and cuts it to 3. It refuses the string "3.50" . So go through a float first. For money, use decimal and skip the rounding surprises: price = "3.50" cents = int ( float ( price ) * 100 ) # parse as float first print ( cents ) from decimal import Decimal # exact money maths print ( int ( Decimal ( price ) * 100 ) ) 3. A Thousands Separator population = "1,250,000" print ( int ( population ) ) # ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '1,250,000' Numbers pasted from a web page or spreadsheet often carry commas. Strip them before you convert. Does your data use a space or a dot instead? Remove that one: population = "1,250,000" print ( int ( population . replace ( "," , "" ) ) ) 4. A Unit or Symbol Next to the Number weight = "72kg" print ( int ( weight ) ) # ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '72kg' Values like 72kg , $5 or 50% have characters that aren't digits. Pull the digits out with a regular expression. Or strip the symbol if you know exactly what it is. Check the regex actually found something, since re.search gives back None when it doesn't: import re weight = "72kg" match = re . search ( r "\d+" , weight ) print ( int ( match . group ( ) ) if match else "no number found" ) 5. A Number in Another Base color = "ff" print ( int ( color ) ) # ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'ff' Unless you say otherwise, int() reads base 10. That's why the message says with base 10 . Hex text like "ff" needs the base as a second argument. Use 16 for hex, 2 for binary and 8 for octal: color = "ff" print ( int ( color , 16 ) ) # tell int() the base: 255 6. A Header or Label Line Mixed In With the Numbers lines = [ "id" , "10" , "20" ] # the first line is a header, not a number total = 0 for line in lines : total += int ( line ) # ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'id' print ( total ) Reading a file line by line? The first line is often a title or header, not data. The message names the culprit, here 'id' . Skip that line. Or let the csv module deal with the header for you: lines = [ "id" , "10" , "20" ] total = 0 for line in lines [ 1 : ] : # skip the header total += int ( line ) print ( total ) The General Fix: Validate Before You Convert If a person typed the text, don't assume it's a number. Keep asking until it is: while True : text = input ( "Age: " ) try : age = int ( text ) break except ValueError : print ( "Please type a whole number, like 25." ) Put only the conversion inside try . That way an unrelated bug won't get swallowed by the same except . And don't rely on text.isdigit() alone. It rejects negatives like "-5" , and it says True for some characters that int() can't convert. The Same Error for float() float() acts the same way, with a different message: ValueError: could not convert string to float: 'abc' . The causes match too. Think empty strings, a comma as the decimal mark ( "3,5" ), a unit or symbol, or a header. The fixes above work here as well. Cleaning Text Before You Convert A few string methods fix most messy input in one line. strip() trims spaces and newlines from both ends, though int() already ignores those. replace() removes separators. split() cuts a line into pieces, and you convert each piece on its own. A small helper keeps all the cleaning in one place: def to_int ( text , default = None ) : cleaned = text . strip ( ) . replace ( "," , "" ) . replace ( "_" , "" ) try : return int ( cleaned ) except ValueError : return default print ( to_int ( "1,250" ) ) # 1250 print ( to_int ( "" ) ) # None print ( to_int ( "abc" , 0 ) ) # 0 Python also allows underscores inside a number, so int("1_000") is 1000. The language permits it. Still, a stray underscore in user input is more likely a typo, so the helper removes it. Returning a default instead of raising is a choice, too. Make it only where you know what a bad value should mean for your program. Quick Reference Text that failed Fix '' (empty) Catch the error, or check for an empty string first '3.50' int(float(text)) , or Decimal for money '1,250,000' text.replace(",", "") '72kg' , '$5' Extract the digits with re.search(r"\d+", text) 'ff' int(text, 16) 'id' or another header Skip the first line, or use csv The Rule, Stated Once ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10 means the string isn't a plain whole number. The message ends with that exact string, so read it first. Then clean it, convert it the right way, or validate before converting. And wrap only the conversion in try/except ValueError . Other Python errors with a clear cause are IndexError: List Index Out of Range , TypeError: NoneType Is Not Subscriptable , IndentationError and UnboundLocalError . New to Python? title: FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory (Fix)
author: Yunus Emre Güzel
summary: You run your script. Python stops and prints this: FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'data.txt' But the file is sitting right there in your folder. So what's going on? Below are the six causes behind this error in real programs. Each one has the exact message it gives and a fix. I ran every example on Python 3.11, 3.12 and 3.14 on Windows. All three print the same message. What the Error Means Your code called open() , and the operating system said it has no file at that path. Look at the end of the message. It shows the path exactly as Python got it, and that's your best clue. Either the name is wrong, or Python is searching a different folder than you think. A path like data.txt with no folder in front is a relative path. Python starts from the current working directory , not from the folder where your script lives. That one detail causes most of these errors. How to Find the Cause Fast Put three lines right before the open() that fails. They show where Python is looking, the full path it built, and whether that path exists: from pathlib import Path import os print ( os . getcwd ( ) ) # the folder Python searches from print ( Path ( "data.txt" ) . resolve ( ) ) # the full path it is trying to open print ( Path ( "data.txt" ) . exists ( ) ) # False means the problem is the path, not your code Is the printed folder not the one holding your file? That's cause 1. Is the folder right? Then compare the file name letter by letter with a listing of the folder. That points to causes 2 and 3. The Six Causes 1. You Ran Python From a Different Folder # Run this from the folder ABOVE this one: python wrong-working-directory/bug.py with open ( "data.txt" ) as f : # relative to where you RUN python, not where the script is print ( f . read ( ) ) Here data.txt is next to the script. But you started the script from the folder above, for example with python wrong-working-directory/bug.py . Some editors do the same when you click Run, because they use the project root. Python then looks in the wrong place. The fix is to build the path from the script's own location. That doesn't care where you run it from: from pathlib import Path here = Path ( __file__ ) . parent # the folder this script lives in with open ( here / "data.txt" ) as f : print ( f . read ( ) ) 2. A Typo in the File Name with open ( "scores.txt" ) as f : # the file is really called score.txt print ( f . read ( ) ) scores.txt and score.txt are two different files. One missing letter is enough. So is a capital letter in the wrong place (names are case sensitive on Linux and macOS), or a space where an underscore should be. Check that the path exists before you open it. If it doesn't, print what's in the folder so the mistake jumps out: from pathlib import Path name = "scores.txt" if not Path ( name ) . exists ( ) : print ( name , "not found. Files here:" , sorted ( p . name for p in Path ( "." ) . iterdir ( ) if p . suffix == ".txt" ) ) else : print ( Path ( name ) . read_text ( ) ) 3. Windows Hid the Real Extension with open ( "notes.txt" ) as f : # Windows hides known extensions: the real name is notes.txt.txt print ( f . read ( ) ) Windows hides the extension of known file types by default. Say you save a file as notes.txt in Notepad. The real name can end up as notes.txt.txt , while Explorer shows notes or notes.txt . You can switch on File name extensions in the Explorer View menu. Or you can list the folder from Python, like in the fix below: from pathlib import Path for p in sorted ( Path ( "." ) . glob ( "notes*" ) ) : # list what is really there, extension included print ( "found:" , p . name ) with open ( "notes.txt.txt" ) as f : # use the real name (or rename the file) print ( f . read ( ) ) 4. Writing to a Folder That Does Not Exist with open ( "output/report.txt" , "w" ) as f : # the folder "output" does not exist yet f . write ( "done" ) People get caught by this one. You're creating the file, so it feels like nothing needs to exist yet. But mode "w" makes the file and never the folders above it. Make the folder first. exist_ok=True keeps it from failing when the folder is already there. parents=True creates several levels at once: from pathlib import Path out = Path ( "output" ) out . mkdir ( exist_ok = True ) # create the folder first ( out / "report.txt" ) . write_text ( "done" ) print ( "wrote" , out / "report.txt" ) 5. A ~ in the Path with open ( "~/notes_demo.txt" , "w" ) as f : # open() does not expand "~" to your home folder f . write ( "hi" ) In a terminal, ~ means your home folder. That's the shell doing the work, not the terminal itself. Python doesn't do it. So open("~/notes.txt") hunts for a folder literally named ~ inside the current directory. Expand it yourself: from pathlib import Path target = Path ( "~/notes_demo.txt" ) . expanduser ( ) # turn "~" into your real home folder target . write_text ( "hi" ) print ( "wrote" , target ) target . unlink ( ) # clean up the demo file 6. Reading a File That Was Never Created with open ( "log.txt" , "r" ) as f : # "r" never creates a file print ( f . read ( ) ) Mode "r" is the default, and it only reads. Say your program creates a log or save file on its first run. Then the very first read fails, because nothing exists yet. Create the file if it's missing. Or open it with "a" (append), which creates it when needed: from pathlib import Path log = Path ( "log.txt" ) if not log . exists ( ) : log . write_text ( "" ) # create it first (or open with "a") with open ( log , "a+" ) as f : f . seek ( 0 ) print ( repr ( f . read ( ) ) ) Related: OSError: [Errno 22] Invalid argument Backslashes in a normal string are escape characters, and that bites on Windows. The path "notes\new_todo.txt" holds a newline, not the letters \n . You won't get FileNotFoundError here. I tested it, and Windows answers OSError: [Errno 22] Invalid argument . The cure is similar to the rest. Use a raw string ( r"C:\temp\test.txt" ), use forward slashes, or build the path with Path . Habits That Prevent It Use pathlib. Path(__file__).parent / "data" / "input.csv" gives you the right path on every system. It doesn't depend on the working directory. Check before you open. Path.exists() and Path.is_file() let you print a clear message instead of a traceback. Catch the error where a missing file is normal , like a settings file on the first run. Handle only that case: from pathlib import Path try : text = Path ( "settings.json" ) . read_text ( ) except FileNotFoundError : text = "{}" # first run: start with defaults Quick Reference Message or situation Fix File is beside the script but not found Path(__file__).parent / "name" Name looks right but fails Compare with sorted(Path(".").iterdir()) ; check case and spaces File was saved from Notepad on Windows Show file name extensions; look for .txt.txt Opening with "w" in a new folder Path(...).mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) first Path starts with ~ Path(...).expanduser() Reading a file the program creates later Create it first, or open with "a" The Rule, Stated Once FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] means the path Python built doesn't exist. So print the working directory and the resolved path. Compare them with where the file really is. Then stop relying on relative names, and build paths from the script's location with pathlib . Want more Python errors with a clear cause? Try KeyError in Python , ValueError: invalid literal for int() , IndexError: List Index Out of Range and ModuleNotFoundError After pip install . title: Lettering machine-translated manga: fitting text back into speech bubbles
author: Leo
summary: When people think about translating manga automatically, they think about the translation model. In practice the translation is the easy part. The hard part is everything around it: finding the text, getting it off the page cleanly, and putting the translation back so the page still reads like a comic. This post walks through the image side of an automatic manga translator I work on, and what we learned by comparing our pages with official English and Korean editions. The pipeline Each page goes through five steps: Find the text. A detector marks the regions that contain text. Page numbers, headers and artist watermarks are not dialogue, so they are left alone. Find the speech bubbles. Knowing the shape of each balloon matters twice: once for cleaning and once for lettering. Read the text. Japanese is often vertical, Korean and Chinese mix scripts, and sound effects are drawn rather than typed. Hand-drawn sound effects outside balloons are usually best left as the artist drew them. Erase the original text. Letter the translation into the cleaned page. Translation sits between steps 3 and 5 and sees the whole page at once, so names and tone stay consistent from bubble to bubble. Erasing is harder than it looks The textbook answer is "mask the text and let an inpainting model fill the hole". On a plain white balloon that often leaves faint gray smudges where the letters used to be, and on screentone or detailed art it can invent texture that wasn't there. What worked better for us was treating different backgrounds differently: plain paper, text with a white outline drawn over artwork, and text sitting on gradients or art each get their own handling. We also make sure that nothing outside the text area changes, so the art around a balloon stays exactly as the artist drew it. Lettering: where it looks human or doesn't Making text fit a box is easy. Making it look lettered is not. A few principles mattered most: Fit the balloon, not the box. Text boxes are rectangles, balloons are ovals. Lines should follow the balloon's shape. Don't shout everything. Filling every balloon to the edge looks wrong next to a professionally lettered page. Ordinary dialogue on a page should look like it was lettered at one size; shouts get to be bigger. Keep words whole. Hyphenating dialogue makes it hard to read, so it should be a last resort. Make sure the font can actually draw the character. Some comic fonts claim to support a character but print nothing, which quietly produces blank bubbles in languages like Thai or Vietnamese. Pick readable colors. Text color guessed from a grayscale scan is often a muddy gray. Black on white (or white on black) is almost always what the original letterer intended. Every language breaks lines differently. English breaks at spaces, Chinese between characters with punctuation rules, Korean at spaces with its own habits for ellipses, and Thai needs a dictionary just to find the words. What we learned Most of the problems only show up at scale. A demo page looks fine; page 40 of a chapter is where a stray gray smudge, a hyphen in the wrong place or a bubble that's slightly too full gives it away. Comparing against official editions, page by page, taught us more than any metric did. Try it If you want to see the result on your own pages, Manga Translator is the web app built on this pipeline: upload a manga, manhwa or webtoon page in the browser and download it lettered in English or 50 other languages. I'd like to hear where the lettering still looks off.

title: How we built an independent search engine on one server
author: nestdaddy
summary: Most "search APIs" are a thin layer over Google or Bing results. NestDaddy is not. It has its own crawler, its own inverted index, its own ranking and its own news collection, and it all runs on a single server with 48 GB of RAM. This post walks through how the pieces fit together, the problems we hit in production, and the numbers we used to decide what to fix. If you are thinking about building search yourself, or you want to know what sits behind the API you are calling, this is for you. The shape of the system There are four parts, and each one is allowed to fail without taking the others down: Crawler. Fetches pages, obeys robots.txt, extracts the readable text and stores it in PostgreSQL. Indexer. Turns new pages into posting lists in a RocksDB index that lives next to the live one. Swap. Once a day, the new index replaces the live index in one atomic step, with an automatic rollback. Search. A BM25 ranker reads the live index, read-only, behind the web site, the REST API and an MCP server for AI agents. The rule that ties them together: the search path never waits for the crawler or the indexer , and neither of them can starve it of CPU or memory. The crawler: polite, bounded, fenced A crawler that misbehaves gets blocked, and a crawler that runs out of memory takes the machine with it. So ours is built around limits. robots.txt first. One fetch per site, cached for 24 hours. A 401 or 403 on robots.txt means "disallow everything". Spread across hosts. Each batch claims URLs from the queue with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED and keeps at most 3 URLs per host. A batch of 500 URLs touches about 500 different sites instead of hammering one. The SKIP LOCKED claim also means several crawler processes can share one queue safely. Bounded downloads. Every response is streamed and cut at 5 MB or 20 seconds. We learned this one the hard way: the first version read response.content and only then trimmed it, so a server that streamed an endless chunked reply pushed the whole body into memory. The fixed version stops at 5.2 MB in 0.07 seconds on the same endless stream. A fence around it. The crawler runs as a systemd service inside its own slice: pinned to 4 of the server's CPUs, capped at 1.5 cores and 3 GB of memory, with a low priority. If it misbehaves, Linux slows it down or stops it, and the search side does not notice. That last point matters more than it sounds. On one day this month the crawler hit its memory cap and restarted 36 times. Search latency, the database and every other service on the machine were untouched. The fence turned a production incident into a log line. The index: RocksDB and posting lists The index is an inverted index stored in RocksDB: for every term, a posting list of document IDs, plus per-document statistics for BM25. We picked RocksDB over a search server for three reasons. It is a library, so there is no extra service to run. It is built for fast point lookups and multi-gets, which is exactly what a query does. And it can be opened read-only by many processes while another process builds the next version. Text goes through a tokenizer (lowercasing, stop words, Porter stemming with a memoised stemmer) before it reaches the index, and the same tokenizer runs on every query. Replacing the index without breaking it Our first pipeline copied index directories while they were open. That produced two corrupted index files before we threw it away. The current swap is boring on purpose: Take the writer lock so the indexer pauses. Hard-link the immutable SST files into a staging directory and copy the small metadata files (MANIFEST, CURRENT, OPTIONS, WAL). This takes about a second and uses no extra disk. Release the lock and verify the staging copy read-only: the document counter must not go down, sample terms must resolve, the newest indexed pages must be readable. Rename the live directory to a "previous" directory and the staging directory to live. Reload the search workers and run a live search check. If anything fails, roll back automatically. Two previous generations are kept, so going back is a rename, not a restore. Ranking: BM25, measured The ranker is BM25 with a few practical additions: a two-stage pre-score (rare terms first, then the top 3,000 candidates re-ranked by term frequency with one RocksDB multi-get), a domain match signal for navigational queries, and image documents kept out of web results. We do not change ranking by feel. A small evaluation set of 40 real queries, each with a judgment ("the right answer is this URL pattern" or "the homepage of this site"), runs against the live index after every change. The fixes we shipped in November moved: Metric Before After Right answer at #1 (P@1) 45% 70% Right answer in the top 3 60% 77.5% Right answer in the top 10 70% 87.5% Mean reciprocal rank 0.536 0.754 The changes behind that were unglamorous: true document frequencies for IDF instead of estimates, an average document length measured from real documents, deterministic sampling instead of random, and keeping images out of web search. Latency: the bugs were not where we expected When search got slow, the ranker was rarely the problem. Profiling live workers found three surprises. A regular expression. The tokenizer stripped email addresses with \S+@\S+ . On some inputs that pattern backtracks quadratically, and one query held the Python GIL for over a minute. The fix was a pattern with identical output and linear time: (?<!\S)(?=\S+@\S)\S+ . The index falling out of RAM. A cold read of the index from disk turned a 0.2 second query into several seconds. We added a small service that checks which parts of the index file are resident ( mincore ) every ten minutes and reads back only what is missing, and we gave it a cgroup memory guarantee so the kernel prefers to evict other files first. One detail cost us an afternoon: cgroup v2 memory protection is hierarchical. Setting MemoryMin on the service did nothing until the parent slice had the same guarantee. A forgotten cron job. Even with that protection, the whole index still vanished from RAM once an hour. The cause was a one-line script in /etc/cron.hourly that ran echo 1 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches , an old "free up memory" trick. Dropping caches ignores cgroup protection entirely. Removing it brought the median query time on our evaluation set from 0.59 seconds back to 0.22 seconds. The lesson we keep relearning: measure on the real machine, and read every scheduled job before you trust a graph. What we have not solved yet Being independent means owning the weak spots too. These are the ones we are working on now: Long, specific queries. The current index weighs titles, descriptions and headings. Pages whose answer lives deep in the body text can rank below a page that merely shares one word with the query. The next index version adds body text, which also means the index outgrows what we can keep in RAM on one machine, so it needs a tiered design first. Numbers and non-Latin scripts. The current tokenizer drops most numbers ("windows 11", "iphone 17") and handles Chinese, Japanese and Thai poorly. A new tokenizer that keeps short numbers and splits CJK and Thai text is written and waiting for the next rebuild. Freshness. Most of the index was crawled months ago. A targeted recrawl of the most searched results and the most linked sites is running now, and the crawler is next in line to run as a continuous pipeline with several processes. Why build it at all Because an index you own is an index nobody can switch off. Microsoft retired the Bing Search APIs in August 2025 and many apps lost their search overnight. Products that need raw results, news by country, or readable page text for AI agents need a source that answers in plain JSON and does not depend on someone else's roadmap. That is what NestDaddy is for. You can try the search, news and page extraction APIs with a free 7-day key at nestdaddy.com/apis , or connect it to Claude, Cursor or any MCP client through nestdaddy.com/mcp . If you have questions about any part of this, or you have built something similar and want to compare notes, we would like to hear from you. Originally published on the NestDaddy blog . title: I built a travel app with Abstract Factory + affiliate APIs — here's what actually worked
author: Sivaraman Ramaswami
summary: I've been building packedNbooked ( https://packednbooked.com ) — a trip planner that starts with your budget instead of a destination. You enter $2,000, JFK, 7 days → it fans out to flight/hotel/car/activity APIs in parallel and returns ranked complete trip packages. This post is about the architecture decisions that held up and the ones that didn't. The pattern: Abstract Factory Every travel category (flights, hotels, cars, attractions) gets its own factory. Each factory spawns provider agents. The orchestrator never touches provider logic directly. class FlightProviderFactory(BaseFactory): def create_agent(self) -> BaseAgent: return TravelpayoutsAgent() class HotelProviderFactory(BaseFactory): def create_agent(self) -> BaseAgent: return BookingAgent() This paid off when I swapped hotel providers mid-project (Hotellook → Booking.com via CJ affiliate). Zero changes to the orchestrator — I just swapped the agent behind the factory. Same when Ticketmaster went live: new factory, new agent, plug it in. The fan-out itself runs async — all four factories fire in parallel, results get budget-pruned, then an LLM (Groq + gpt-oss-120b) ranks the combos by value. The hotel API nightmare This is the part nobody writes about. My original plan was real-time hotel pricing. Here's what I found: Amadeus — decommissioned their free tier in July 2025 Travelpayouts hotel endpoints — all 404 Booking.com, Agoda, Expedia, HotelBeds — all require commercial contracts Booking.com via CJ affiliate — Demand API is restricted to "strategic partners," no application path I spent three weeks on this before accepting the ceiling: mock prices + live Booking.com deep-links is the permanent setup. The links go to Booking.com search results where users see real availability. It's honest — I label prices as estimates and the Show HN caveat was upfront about it. The lesson: travel pricing APIs are a moat. If you're not paying enterprise rates, you're not getting real-time hotel data. Build around it, not through it. The affiliate setup (actual numbers) Revenue model is affiliate commissions — no ads, no paywall: Partner Integration Notes Travelpayouts/Aviasales Live prices via Data API marker 326901 Booking.com via CJ Deep-links, mock prices publisher 101876939 Viator Live affiliate links ID P00319033 DiscoverCars Affiliate link ~$20/booking, 365-day cookie Booking.com's CJ approval took about a week. Viator was instant. DiscoverCars was the fastest approval and best cookie window. Realistic projection: $0–20/mo now, $200–430/mo at 20k monthly visitors. It's a long game — the affiliate revenue only matters if the SEO compounds. What's actually live FastAPI backend on Railway ($5/mo), React/Vite frontend on Render (free static) Flights: real cached prices from Travelpayouts /v2/prices/latest Hotels: estimated prices, live Booking.com deep-links Attractions: Viator (live) + Ticketmaster Discovery API (real events by city/date) AI ranking: falls back to cost-sort if Groq key is missing 115 tests passing What I'd do differently Start with the affiliate approvals. I wired affiliate links at the end and retroactively got approvals. Should have done it week one — some take a week+, and you don't want to build around a partner that rejects you. Don't fight the hotel API wall. I lost three weeks trying to find real-time hotel pricing. The correct answer was always "mock prices + live booking link." Abstract Factory was the right call. The pattern felt like over-engineering for a solo project at first. It wasn't — I swapped providers three times without touching orchestration logic. App is live at https://packednbooked.com . Code isn't public yet but happy to answer questions about the architecture or affiliate setup. What travel pricing APIs have you found that actually work at the free/indie tier?

title: Slack answers 200 OK when your message did not go out
author: Greg Pabijan-Morawski
summary: Here is a complete, successful HTTP exchange with Slack: POST https : //slack.com/api/chat.postMessage Authorization : Bearer xoxb - … HTTP / 1.1 200 OK { "ok" : false , "error" : "not_in_channel" } The message did not go anywhere. The status line says it did. If your code does what most HTTP code does — if (res.ok) return; — every failure Slack can describe to you looks exactly like success. We just built Slack, Teams, Discord and Google Chat delivery into Pulsenote, and almost none of the work was sending. It was reading the answer. Why the Web API at all The quick way to post to Slack used to be an incoming-webhook URL: paste it, POST some JSON, done. Slack is retiring the old Incoming WebHooks integration, and the way in that it points you to now is a small app in your own workspace: create it at api.slack.com/apps, give it the chat:write scope, install it, and you get a bot token starting with xoxb- . With that token you call chat.postMessage . The webhook endpoint answers with HTTP status codes, like a normal service. The Web API does not. Apart from rate limits and outages, it answers 200 and puts the verdict in the body. So the first rule of our Slack sender is in its doc comment: /** The Web API answers 200 with `ok: false` for most errors; HTTP status only for 429 and outages. */ export function classifySlackApi ( res : HttpResult ) : DestinationDelivery { if ( res . status === 429 || res . status >= 500 ) { return classifyResponse ( DestinationType . SLACK , res ) ; } // …parse the body, then decide on `ok` and `error` } Three outcomes, not two Once you are reading the answer properly, "worked / didn't" turns out to be too coarse. A failed delivery means one of three things, and each needs a different response: export type DestinationDelivery = | { status : 'sent' } /** The URL will never work again — the destination must be marked broken. */ | { status : 'broken' ; reason : string } /** Did not go out. `retry` says whether trying the same bytes later can help. */ | { status : 'failed' ; reason : string ; retry : boolean ; retryAfterS ?: number } ; Try again later. A 429, a 5xx, a timeout, Slack's own ratelimited code. The platform is having a bad minute; the same request will work later. Give up on this message. Any other 4xx. The receiver looked at these bytes and said no. Sending the identical bytes again will be refused again, and it tells you nothing about whether the destination still works for the next message. The comment in our code says exactly that, because the temptation to retry it is strong. The destination is dead. The app was uninstalled, the token revoked, the channel archived, the bot never invited. Every future message will fail the same way. Retrying is pointless; what you need is a person to fix something — and they need to be told what . That last group is where Slack's error codes earn their keep. They are specific enough to turn into instructions: const SLACK_APP_BROKEN : Record < string , string > = { token_revoked : 'The app was removed from the workspace or its token was revoked.' , missing_scope : 'The app is missing the chat:write scope. Add it under OAuth & Permissions and reinstall.' , not_in_channel : 'The app is not in that channel. Invite it there with /invite @your-app, or add the chat:write.public scope.' , is_archived : 'That Slack channel is archived.' , // …and a few more } ; When one of these comes back, we mark the destination broken with that sentence as the reason, and any further send to it is refused straight away with a 422 that carries it, instead of joining a queue that will never drain. A successful test send clears the flag. For the platforms that do use status codes — Teams, Discord, Google Chat, a plain webhook — the same rule reads 404 and 410 as "this URL is gone". Check the token before you keep it The cheapest place to find a bad token is the form where someone pastes it. Slack has a method for exactly this, auth.test , which costs nothing and returns the workspace name when the token is good. We call it before saving, so a copy-paste mistake fails in front of the person who made it, not at 3 a.m. on the first real alert. We also refuse a token starting with xoxp- with a specific message. It is a user token, it works, and it posts as that person — which is not what anyone wanted for an order notification. Every platform has its own trap Slack's 200 is the most surprising, but it is not the only one. Discord pings people. A message containing @everyone that you forwarded from user input will notify the whole server. Every Discord message we send carries allowed_mentions: { parse: [] } , which turns that off. Discord also stops at 2,000 characters per message, so we cut there rather than have the whole message refused. Teams changed its front door. The Office 365 connector URLs on *.webhook.office.com are being retired by Microsoft; incoming webhooks now come from Workflows, on Power Automate hosts. We only accept the new shape, because a URL that works today and stops on Microsoft's schedule is a support ticket with a date on it. Teams also wants an Adaptive Card wrapped in a message envelope, not a bare text field. Your own endpoint cannot tell a retry from a second message unless you give it something to compare. Every webhook body carries the message id, and every request is signed ( X-Pulsenote-Signature: sha256=… , an HMAC of the raw body). Retries belong in the database The retry schedule — 10 seconds, 1 minute, 5 minutes, 30 minutes, five attempts in all — is stored on the message row, not in a timer: /** * The retry schedule lives on the row, not in memory, so a deploy in the * middle of a Slack outage loses nothing. */ That is the failure that in-process retry loops hide: they work in every test and lose messages exactly when the platform is down and you ship a fix for it. When the platform sends Retry-After , we wait that long instead (capped at ten minutes, so a bad header cannot park a message for a day). "Sent" is still not "delivered" One more thing we were careful about. When Slack says ok: true , our record says SENT — and never DELIVERED . For email, "delivered" means a receiving mail server accepted the message, and our abuse checks and deliverability warnings are computed from it. A chat message counted as an email delivery would quietly make those rates look healthier than they are. Two facts, one word again, in a new place. What to do on Monday If you call the Slack Web API, read ok in the body. The status code will not tell you. Sort failures into retry , drop this message and destination dead . Only the first deserves a retry; only the last deserves a human. Turn the platform's error code into a sentence a person can act on, and show it where they will see it. Validate credentials when they are entered, not when they are first used. Turn off mentions for any text you did not write yourself. Keep the retry schedule somewhere that survives a restart. If you would rather not write those six things, this is what Pulsenote destinations do — the same API key and the same log as your email. But the list is worth having either way: the hard part of sending a chat message was never the sending.

title: AI Won’t Replace You. It’s Moving Your Code From the Screen to the Contract
author: Fausto Braz
summary: Every few weeks, someone posts an impressive agent demo, and the replies fill up with the same prediction: developers are done. Teams will shrink to one person and a model, and that one person will be cheap. I'm a frontend developer, mostly Angular, and I'm genuinely excited about what agents can do. Recently, I watched a livestream where someone used CopilotKit to build an app that turns plain prompts into charts. Impressive stuff. But the question that stuck with me wasn't "is my job over?" It was: who decided which charts it was allowed to draw? I'm also tired of the "devs are done" story. Not because I think nothing will change. A lot will. But when I stopped reading hot takes and started reading the specs behind the agent stack, I found something that the crowd keeps skipping: these protocols create a lot of engineering work. It just isn't the work we're used to. This week gave me a good excuse to write it down. On November 11, Google shipped A2UI 1.0 , the first stable version of its open protocol for agent-generated UI. Atlassian is bringing it to Jira, and Bloomberg and ByteDance are building with it. Its sibling, A2A , the protocol agents use to talk to each other, reached v1.0 earlier this year under the Linux Foundation. Here's my argument in one line: these protocols don't remove the code. They move it from the screen to the contract. The map: four boundaries, four protocols "Agentic app" sounds like one thing. In practice, it's a set of boundaries, and each one now has its own protocol: Boundary Protocol What crosses it Who designs it Agent ↔ agent A2A tasks, messages, artifacts backend Agent ↔ tools and data MCP tool calls, resources backend Agent ↔ app AG-UI events, state, user actions full-stack Agent → screen A2UI a declarative description of UI frontend A quick tour: A2A lets an agent discover another agent through an Agent Card , a JSON document published at /.well-known/agent-card.json . It can then hand that agent a task and follow it through a lifecycle: submitted , working , input-required , auth-required , completed , failed , and so on. It runs over JSON-RPC, gRPC, or plain HTTP+JSON. MCP is how an agent reaches tools and data. You probably know this one already. AG-UI , from the CopilotKit team, is the event stream between your app and an agent backend: messages, shared state, tool calls and user actions. A2UI is the new piece. The agent doesn't send HTML or JavaScript. It sends JSON that says "put a chart here, bound to this data", and your app renders it with your components. That JSON can travel over AG-UI, over A2A (as an extension) or inside MCP. Look at the last column of the table. Every row has an owner, and none of them is "the model". Frontend: from screens to vocabulary This is the part of A2UI that changed my mind. An agent can only use components that exist in a catalog , and the catalog belongs to the client. The A2UI basic catalog gives you primitives like Text , Row , Column , Button and TextField . Anything more specific, like a chart in your brand colours that handles empty states and keyboard navigation, is a component you write and register. That turns the catalog into something new: a public API whose consumer is a language model. Everything you'd do for a good component library still applies, plus some new questions: What is the agent allowed to ask for? A2UI catalogs can restrict which components nest inside which ( allowedChildren , allowedParents ) and which side may call which function ( allowedCallers ). That isn't styling. It's a security boundary, and the frontend team owns it. How do you describe a component so a model uses it well? Catalogs carry their own guidance for the model. Naming props and documenting them becomes a form of prompt design. How do you guarantee quality you can't review screen by screen? When layouts are assembled at runtime, accessibility, loading and error states, and performance budgets can't be checked in a pull request for each screen. They have to live inside the components. Even the vendors mix approaches. In CopilotKit's open-source Open Intelligent UI , simple tables are rendered through A2UI, while charts, maps and calculators go through a separate path that streams generated UI into a sandboxed iframe. Someone had to decide which kind of UI each moment deserves and what risk each option carries. That decision is architecture, and no model made it for them. So, back to my livestream question: who decides which charts an agent can draw? With A2UI, whoever owns the catalog. With an open-ended iframe, the model does, but inside a sandbox that a person designed. Either way, a developer made the call. Backend: from endpoints to capabilities On the backend, A2A changes the unit of design. You're no longer just exposing GET /expenses . You're publishing capabilities , listed as skills in an Agent Card, that other agents will discover and call, possibly from other teams or other companies. The hard problems don't go away. They turn into distributed-systems problems: Long-running work. A task can pause in input-required while it waits for a human, or in auth-required while it waits for credentials, and then resume. Someone has to model those states, the timeouts and the retries. Trust. Which agents may call yours, and how do you know an agent is who it claims to be? A2A supports OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect, mutual TLS, and signed Agent Cards. Choosing and wiring those is real work, and getting it wrong is real exposure. Keeping data away from the model. A2UI 1.0 can bind data on the server, so sensitive values reach the screen without ever entering the model's context. Deciding what the model sees, and what it never sees, is a design decision with legal consequences. Observability. When one user request hops across three agents, and one of them misbehaves, someone has to trace it. None of this is "write less code and think about product instead". It's harder code, in places where architecture and product decisions can't be separated. Where this doesn't fit, and what really goes away I'd be selling hype myself if I stopped there, so here's the honest part. Some work does shrink. Hand-building yet another CRUD screen, filter panel or settings form: much of that will be composed by agents from good catalogs. If that's the only thing you do, your job is changing. Generative UI isn't always better. A checkout, a regulated form, anything where users rely on muscle memory: those want a predictable interface. Sonu Kapoor argues in InfoWorld that generative UI needs component systems rather than code generated at runtime, and there are thoughtful posts on why generative UI doesn't make sense for many startups and on what actually works in production . It's early. A2UI 1.0 is days old. Some renderers were still on v0.9.x when it was announced, and the tooling moves fast: CopilotKit archived its generative UI playground repo in October. Look closely at those objections, though. Each one is an argument for more engineering judgement, not less: knowing when generative UI is the wrong tool, building the components it depends on, and deciding where the boundaries go. A concrete example: "Show me travel spend by person" Here's a small scenario that puts all the pieces together. I'll build it end to end in Part 2. Picture a team expenses app. The user types: "Show me this quarter's travel spend, by person." An orchestrator agent receives the request. It doesn't own finance data, so it delegates the task through A2A to a finance agent , which could be built by another team or another company. The finance agent answers with A2UI : a card with a bar chart. The bar chart isn't in the basic catalog. It's a component the frontend team added to the app's own catalog. When the user changes the period, that action goes back to the agent and the chart updates. The amounts reach the chart through data binding , not through the model's text. And the form to submit a new expense? A plain Angular reactive form. Predictable, validated, and boring, on purpose. Here's the finance agent's Agent Card, trimmed. The A2UI extension tells other agents which UI vocabularies this agent can speak: { "name" : "Finance Agent" , "description" : "Answers questions about team expenses and budgets." , "version" : "1.0.0" , "supportedInterfaces" : [ { "url" : "https://finance.example.com/a2a" , "protocolBinding" : "JSONRPC" , "protocolVersion" : "1.0" } ] , "capabilities" : { "streaming" : true , "extensions" : [ { "uri" : "https://a2ui.org/a2a-extension/a2ui/v1.0" , "required" : false , "params" : { "supportedCatalogIds" : [ "https://example.com/a2ui/expenses-catalog.json" ] } } ] } , "defaultInputModes" : [ "text/plain" ] , "defaultOutputModes" : [ "text/plain" ] , "skills" : [ { "id" : "spend-report" , "name" : "Spend report" , "description" : "Summarises spend by person, category or period." , "tags" : [ "finance" , "reporting" ] } ] } What the finance agent sends back isn't HTML. It's a short stream of A2UI messages that describe the UI: { "version" : "1.0" , "createSurface" : { "surfaceId" : "travel_spend" , "catalogId" : "https://example.com/a2ui/expenses-catalog.json" } } { "version" : "1.0" , "updateComponents" : { "surfaceId" : "travel_spend" , "components" : [ { "id" : "root" , "component" : "Column" , "children" : [ "title" , "chart" ] } , { "id" : "title" , "component" : "Text" , "text" : "Travel spend, Q4" } , { "id" : "chart" , "component" : "BarChart" , "chartData" : { "@path" : "/spend" } } ] } } { "version" : "1.0" , "updateDataModel" : { "surfaceId" : "travel_spend" , "path" : "/spend" , "value" : [ { "label" : "Ana" , "value" : 1840 } , { "label" : "Rui" , "value" : 960 } ] } } Three details are worth noticing: The components are a flat list with IDs, not a nested tree. That suits a model that streams tokens: pieces can arrive in any order, and the renderer waits until a root exists before drawing. The layout and the data travel separately. The model decides what to show. The numbers go into a data model that, in a real setup, the agent's server can fill straight from the finance system. BarChart only works because someone built it. That someone is the frontend team, and this is what their side looks like in Angular: // bar-chart.ts (simplified from the official A2UI "authoring components" guide) import { Component , computed } from '@angular/core' ; import { AngularCatalog , BASIC_COMPONENTS , BASIC_FUNCTIONS , CatalogComponent } from '@a2ui/angular/v0_9' ; import { ComponentApi } from '@a2ui/web_core/v0_9' ; import { BaseChartDirective } from 'ng2-charts' ; import { z } from 'zod' ; // 1. The contract: what the agent can ask for. export const BarChartApi = { name : 'BarChart' , schema : z . object ( { title : z . string ( ) . optional ( ) , chartData : z . array ( z . object ( { label : z . string ( ) , value : z . number ( ) } ) ) , } ) . strict ( ) , } satisfies ComponentApi ; // 2. The implementation: your design system, your accessibility rules. @Component ( { selector : 'app-bar-chart' , imports : [ BaseChartDirective ] , template : `<canvas baseChart type="bar" [data]="chartData()"></canvas>` , } ) export class BarChart extends CatalogComponent < typeof BarChartApi > { protected readonly chartData = computed ( ( ) => { const rows = this . props ( ) [ 'chartData' ] ? . value ( ) ?? [ ] ; return { labels : rows . map ( ( r ) => r . label ) , datasets : [ { data : rows . map ( ( r ) => r . value ) } ] , } ; } ) ; } // 3. The vocabulary: everything an agent can render in this app. export const EXPENSES_CATALOG = new AngularCatalog ( 'https://example.com/a2ui/expenses-catalog.json' , [ . . . BASIC_COMPONENTS , { . . . BarChartApi , component : BarChart } ] , BASIC_FUNCTIONS , ) ; That BarChartApi schema is the contract. The agent can't ask for a PieChart nobody built. It can't pass a prop nobody declared, thanks to .strict() . When it gets something wrong, the renderer rejects the message and reports an error back to the agent. The model writes the request, but the frontend team decides what's possible. A note on versions: these snippets use the Angular renderer's current v0_9 entry point. Renderer packages for 1.0 are rolling out, so check the A2UI docs before you copy anything. What to learn next If you're on the frontend: Treat your design system as an API: strict prop contracts, schemas, and documentation written for a model as well as for people. Pick one A2UI renderer (Angular, React, Lit or Flutter) and build one custom catalog component end to end. Put accessibility and every state (loading, empty, error) inside your components, because nobody will review each generated screen. If you're on the backend: Read the task lifecycle and security sections of the A2A spec . Model a task that pauses for human input and resumes. Learn the auth options (OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect, mutual TLS) and what signed Agent Cards protect against. Practise drawing the line between data the model sees and data it never touches. For both: learn to choose. A predefined component, a declarative A2UI surface, a sandboxed open-ended UI, or no generative UI at all. Making that call well, for each moment of a product, is the job. The job didn't disappear. It moved. The "AI will replace developers" story assumes our job is typing code into screens. Read A2A and A2UI closely, and you see the opposite. Agents are only as good as the contracts, catalogs, and boundaries someone designs for them. That someone needs product sense and architectural judgement, and still has to write code very well. If you've already shipped generative UI, I'd love to hear what broke and what surprised you, in the comments. title: Keep PDF Cleanup in the Browser Before Calling a Translation API
author: Reid Marlow
summary: When someone drops a contract, pay stub, or hardware datasheet into a free web PDF editor to delete a few pages or fill a form, most tools send the full document to a remote server before showing a preview. TechRepublic's November 10, 2026 review of free PDF editors shows why that habit persists. Referring back to a May 31, 2026 policy audit across eight major web converters and editors (Smallpdf, iLovePDF, Adobe Acrobat online, PDF24 online, CloudConvert, Sejda, Convertio, and TinyPNG), every single service uploaded documents to remote servers. Their stated retention windows run from around one hour to 48 hours, paired with free caps like 3 tasks per hour on Sejda online or 1 free task every 30 days on Adobe Acrobat online. For developers and technical teams, the usual workaround is installing a desktop app or self-hosting a container like Stirling PDF just to slice pages or patch text. That works, though spinning up a service feels heavy for a two-minute edit. Separate local cleanup from remote compute Most PDF chores break into two separate jobs. First comes local structural prep: extracting specific pages, removing sensitive appendices, reordering sections, running find-and-replace, filling forms, signing, and exporting. Second comes heavy server-side transformation, such as layout-preserving translation across multi-column documents, embedded tables, or text inside images. Classic web utilities bundle both into a single remote upload. Sending an unedited 90-page PDF to a cloud server just to keep six pages leaks unnecessary context and hits task caps early. How KomoPDF splits the workflow KomoPDF is a no-sign-up browser PDF editor organized around that split. Content editing, find and replace, page organization and extraction, form filling, signing, export, and printing run locally in the browser so files stay on the device. When a document needs layout-preserving translation across any of nine supported languages, the sidebar offers an optional connection to KolmoPDF . Connecting a KolmoPDF API key keeps that key for the browser session, lets you pick a translated PDF or bilingual side-by-side output (with toggles for image text, tables, and an optional glossary CSV), and uploads only the current edited PDF version to KolmoPDF at 2 credits per page without replacing the original file. Pruning a document locally first changes two things in practice: sensitive pages stripped out in the browser never leave the machine when translation runs, and trimming an 80-page specification down to the five pages a team needs drops a 160-credit translation run to 10 credits. Knowing where local ends and upload begins Calling a tool "private" hides the real engineering boundary when it mixes client-side utilities with hosted AI features. On KomoPDF, local editing, page extraction, forms, signing, and printing stay on the user's device, while enabling KolmoPDF translation explicitly uploads the active document version to that external service. Keeping those two steps separate lets teams keep routine PDF work off remote servers and opt into cloud translation only on the exact pages that need it.

title: From an AI-visibility score to a GEO action plan: what to fix first
author: Wader Zhang
summary: A score only helps if it tells you what to do next. Here's how to read an AI-visibility result and turn it into fixes, in the order that usually matters most. Disclosure: we build KiteGEO; the examples use its report format, but the steps apply to any tool. Read the score as three separate problems KiteGEO's GEO score is 60% visibility, 20% reputation and 20% AI readiness. Each part points to a different fix: Low visibility (assistants don't name you for unbranded buyer questions): you're missing from the places assistants learn about your category. Low reputation (they don't know you, or describe you wrongly): there isn't enough clear, consistent information about you. Low AI readiness (crawlers can't read your site): a technical problem, usually the quickest to fix. Fix 1: let AI crawlers read your site Check that robots.txt doesn't block AI search crawlers (OAI-SearchBot, Claude-SearchBot, PerplexityBot). Blocking training-only crawlers such as GPTBot or Google-Extended is a legitimate opt-out and doesn't stop assistants reading you for search answers. Make sure your main pages work without JavaScript, and add an llms.txt and schema.org data (Organization, Product or SoftwareApplication, FAQPage). Fix 2: say plainly what you are Assistants repeat what's clear and consistent. Have one plain sentence of what you offer, for whom, and how you differ, and use it on your home page, About page, structured data and profiles. Answer common buyer questions on your site in an FAQ. Fix 3: be present where the assistants look This is the one most teams skip, and it's usually the biggest lever. Look at the sources the assistants cite for your buyer questions: comparison articles, "best X" lists, Reddit and Quora threads, Zhihu, industry blogs, directories. If competitors are there and you aren't, that's your gap. Publish honest, useful articles that answer the questions you lose, on sites assistants read. Answer real forum questions helpfully, disclosing that you work on the product. Get listed in the directories and comparisons that are cited for your category. Fix 4: correct what's wrong If an assistant describes you inaccurately, fix the source: update your own pages, profiles and listings so the correct facts appear consistently. Then measure, weekly Rerun the same questions every week. Visibility usually moves over weeks, not days, as new pages get read and cited. On paid plans, the publishing toolkit then finds the sites and threads AI cites for your category each week, drafts the articles and answers, posts to connected sites, and shows whether the assistants start citing them. We're using it on ourselves: in November 2026 KiteGEO's site scored 100/100 for AI readiness while the assistants named it in only 4% of buyer answers. Fix 3 is our job now. title: Where the 150 seconds actually go: profiling a local render loop
author: mujin
summary: Splitting the 150 seconds into model load, sampling steps, and PNG encode with a stopwatch and cProfile, in a script short enough to paste My SD1.5 render loop runs in fp32 with model offload on a 4GB GTX 1650. A 512x768 image takes about 150 seconds, but that total does not identify the bottleneck. I used perf_counter for the boundaries I control and cProfile for calls inside Diffusers. The script assumes the model is already cached locally, so network activity cannot contaminate model-load time. import cProfile import io import os from pathlib import Path from time import perf_counter import torch from diffusers import StableDiffusionPipeline wall_start = perf_counter ( ) profiler = cProfile . Profile ( ) profiler . enable ( ) load_start = perf_counter ( ) pipe = StableDiffusionPipeline . from_pretrained ( os . environ [ "MODEL" ] , torch_dtype = torch . float32 , local_files_only = True , ) pipe . enable_model_cpu_offload ( ) model_load = perf_counter ( ) - load_start step_marks = [ ] def mark_step ( pipe , step , timestep , callback_kwargs ) : step_marks . append ( perf_counter ( ) ) return callback_kwargs sample_start = perf_counter ( ) image , * _ = pipe ( prompt = os . environ [ "PROMPT" ] , width = 512 , height = 768 , callback_on_step_end = mark_step , ) . images sample_end = step_marks . pop ( ) if step_marks else perf_counter ( ) sampling_steps = sample_end - sample_start png_start = perf_counter ( ) buffer = io . BytesIO ( ) image . save ( buffer , format = "PNG" ) png_encode = perf_counter ( ) - png_start Path ( os . environ [ "OUTPUT" ] ) . write_bytes ( buffer . getvalue ( ) ) profiler . disable ( ) wall_seconds = perf_counter ( ) - wall_start profiler . dump_stats ( "render.prof" ) print ( { "model_load" : model_load , "sampling_steps" : sampling_steps , "png_encode" : png_encode , "wall_seconds" : wall_seconds , } ) I inspect the profile with: python -m pstats render.prof sort cumtime stats The stopwatch gives stable phase boundaries. cProfile then shows whether time inside the sampling phase belongs to model execution, scheduler work, tensor transfers, or Python callbacks. I keep wall time as the control because the phase totals intentionally omit some setup and file-write overhead. What the profile changed: the two fixes that cut wall-clock, and the one “optimization” that only moved the cost to disk Fix A was moving pipeline construction outside the per-image function. The daemon now loads SD1.5 once, enables model offload once, and reuses the pipeline. This removes repeated model loading from subsequent renders without pretending that loading became faster. Fix B was eliminating a PNG round trip. The old path saved the image, reopened it to calculate the content hash, and then read it again for the next pipeline stage. The current path encodes once into BytesIO . The same byte string is hashed and written to disk. The false optimization was avoiding PNG compression by writing a large intermediate image. CPU time fell, but file-write time and storage traffic increased. The profile looked better only when I stopped measuring before the write. End-to-end wall time did not receive the same benefit. The decision rule is simple: an optimization stays only if wall_seconds falls when measured from the same start and end points. A faster inner function is not sufficient. The single per-run number worth writing to a text file, so a slow week is visible before it is a mystery I record total wall seconds for every successful 512x768 render. I do not use sampling time alone because that would hide regressions in model loading, encoding, or disk writes. with open ( "render-wall-seconds.txt" , "a" , encoding = "utf-8" ) as log : log . write ( f "{wall_seconds}\n" ) This file is deliberately plain. It works with shell tools, survives daemon restarts, and makes a sustained slowdown visible without requiring a monitoring service. The detailed profile is diagnostic output; total wall time is the trend. The rendered work feeds the collection at https://thunderous-sunflower-a910b4.netlify.app , but the same measurement applies to any local image pipeline. Practical takeaway: wrap your render at the process boundary, append total wall seconds to a text file, and reject any optimization that improves only an internal timer.
