title: There Is No Third Auction. Your Foreclosure Math Is Wrong Twice.
author: Jiahui Miao
summary: TL;DR: Most explainers describe China's court foreclosure sales as a three-auction staircase: first auction, second auction, third auction, then a sale by listing. That staircase belongs to the old traditional-auction rules. Under the current online judicial auction rules, there are exactly two auctions. The first must start at no less than 70 percent of the appraised value. If nobody bids, a second auction follows within 30 days, with a cut of no more than 20 percent. If that fails too, the property moves to a listing sale. There is no third auction — and anyone pricing a deal off the wrong staircase has the wrong timeline by 30 to 60 days and the wrong price floor by 8 points. Start with the floor, because it is where the bad math compounds. Multiply the two legal extremes — 70 percent, then another 20 percent off — and you get 56 percent of appraised value. That number circulates as if it were the price foreclosures clear at. It is not a price. It is the extreme that occurs only if a court pushes both steps to the statutory minimum. In the first ten months of 2026, residential foreclosures in China actually sold at 79.0 percent of appraised value, across the whole market. In a worked Shenzhen example from the same data, the second auction opened at 64.0 percent of appraisal and was bid back up to a sale at 73.0 percent. Courts often do not push the first step to the floor at all. Anchor a negotiation on 56 percent and you will not sound disciplined. You will sound uninformed, in every negotiation, all year. The second error is treating the appraisal as a market price with a discount attached. If homes clear at 79 percent of appraisal as a national average, the appraisal itself is systematically high — by roughly a fifth to a quarter. The discount rate is not a national constant either. It is a function of city tier and property type, and the spread is not subtle. What the clearance data actually says Clearance rate — sold units divided by listings whose sale window has closed, not by everything ever listed — tells you which assets the endgame market will absorb at all. For January to October 2026: residential cleared at 38.4 percent, industrial at 24.5 percent, land at 22.5 percent, commercial at 16.3 percent, and parking spaces at 9.2 percent. The residential unit and the shop on its ground floor live in different liquidity worlds: a 2.4-times difference in clearance and an 11-point difference in discount depth, in the same building. Underwrite a commercial unit with residential exit assumptions and the model is fiction before the first payment. Volume is the third misreading. Listings rose 31.6 percent and completed sales rose 34.6 percent by count — but only 19.0 percent by value. Do the division and the average sold unit fell about 11.6 percent. That is not a recovery. That is a market clearing inventory by cutting price: more units, less money per unit. Reading rising foreclosure volume as a warming market, and raising your offers into it, is the most expensive interpretation error available this year. One honest caveat: these are one research institute's database figures, reported in full by two financial outlets — not a court-published census — and city-level clearance and discount rates for the two cities I work in most were not in the public release. Until I compute them from my own sample, I label every use of the national 79 percent as a national figure, not a local measurement. What I changed in my own underwriting I do not bid at these auctions. My real estate work is pre-foreclosure: negotiating a direct takeover with the owner before the staircase runs. Which is exactly why the staircase matters to me — not as a buying channel, but as a public clock and a public ruler. A failed first auction is a free referendum. The market has just announced, in public, that 70 percent of appraisal was too much. The court says to the owner what I could never say credibly across a table. So my outreach is now sequenced by the ladder, not by debt size: first contact within seven days of a failed first auction, a second touch when the second auction is announced, and the listing-sale phase treated as the best-evidenced window of all. My data layer now records, for every property, which regime it is under and which step it sits on — read from the court's own notice, never assumed — because the two regimes differ by a month of timeline and 8 points of floor. And commercial and parking assets no longer pass through my intake on residential exit assumptions; at 16.3 and 9.2 percent clearance, they need their own exit story, in writing, or they do not pass. The staircase is a pricing machine built out of deadlines. Most commentary reads it as a discount chart and gets both the steps and the floor wrong. Read it as a clock instead: value does not slide down it smoothly — it falls in steps, on published dates, in public. The negotiation is won by whoever shows up right after a step lands. — Jiahui Miao, founder of vertciti, building a personal AI operating system for one.

title: 116,000 Stars vs. One Binary: claude-mem and palace-rs, Fact by Fact
author: iCe Gaming
summary: claude-mem is the most popular memory plugin for AI coding agents. At the time of writing it has 116,434 GitHub stars . palace-rs does the same job. It has 10 . Stars tell you what people clicked. They don't tell you what you have to install, what runs in the background, who writes your memories, or whether anyone measured if the thing finds the right memory. So I went through both projects' own READMEs, docs and source and wrote down what each one actually does. Every claim below links back to something you can open. No guesses. What you install claude-mem (from its README and package.json , v15.18.1): Node.js ^20.19.0 || >=22.12.0 Bun >=1.1.31 , "JavaScript runtime and process manager" uv , "Python package manager for vector search" Chroma , enabled by default ( CLAUDE_MEM_CHROMA_ENABLED: 'true' ), run locally as chroma-mcp through uvx A worker , "a local HTTP service managed by Bun", that takes tool activity from hooks, runs the observer, and serves the viewer and search That's a JavaScript runtime, a second JavaScript runtime, a Python toolchain, a vector database and a long-running HTTP service. palace-rs (from its README, v0.20.0): One binary, one SQLite file, no API keys, no cloud. No Python, no vector database, no Docker. One palace executable and one palace.db file. Embeddings run on your CPU through ONNX Runtime. There's no server process to keep alive. The install script downloads the release binary, verifies its SHA-256 checksum, and you run palace install to wire up your agents. Who writes your memories This is the biggest difference, and it's a design choice, not a detail. claude-mem uses an LLM to write your memory. In its own words: Hooks in your agent hand each tool call (what it reads, edits and runs) to a small local worker. A second agent turns that activity into short observations, and writes a summary when the session ends. The default settings in SettingsDefaultsManager.ts are CLAUDE_MEM_PROVIDER: 'claude' and CLAUDE_MEM_MODEL: 'haiku' . So what ends up in memory is a model's summary of what happened, not what happened. That second agent also has to be paid for by someone. The README lists three options: the hosted "claude-mem observer" (a 30-day free trial that asks for a payment method), your own OpenRouter or Gemini key, or your Anthropic plan. It then says: With the observer, memory runs off-plan, so you get up to 100% more usage from your plan. Read that the other way round: when memory runs on your plan, it's using your plan. And when the trial ends, "memory automatically falls back to your Anthropic plan unless you subscribe." palace-rs stores text verbatim and uses no LLM. Code, notes, and conversations are stored as written, not as an LLM summary that loses detail. No API key, no model calls, no second agent, no subscription. Recall is hybrid search (BM25 fused with cosine similarity over local embeddings) plus intent-aware ranking. A local cross-encoder reranker is optional. Nothing in the memory path costs tokens to create. Does it find the right memory? A memory tool has one job: when the agent needs something from last week, return it. palace-rs publishes its numbers. On LongMemEval s_cleaned (470 evaluated questions, each over a haystack of about 50 sessions and 115k tokens), stored the way Palace actually stores conversations: Metric palace-rs R@1 0.915 R@5 0.987 R@10 0.996 From the README's method notes: "No LLM at any stage, no GPU." The one ranking weight picked on LongMemEval data was chosen on a different split ( m_cleaned ) and frozen before the run. Per-question-type results are published too, including the weakest category. It also ships a coding-agent eval (51 questions like "why did we choose bundled sqlite?") that runs with one command: cargo test --test coding_agent_eval -- --nocapture The README says plainly that this eval is partly tuned, and prints the untuned numbers next to the tuned ones. claude-mem's README publishes no retrieval benchmark. There's no LongMemEval score, no recall@K, no eval command. The token figures it does give ("~50-100 tokens/result" for the index, "~500-1,000 tokens/result" for full details) come with its own disclaimer: The ratio is not a measured recall or end-to-end saving. So for the most-starred memory tool in this space, there's no published number for how often it returns the right memory. For the 10-star one, there is, with the command to reproduce it. Recall that doesn't depend on the agent remembering to search Both tools use hooks. palace-rs installs four: Session start injects your standing rules, recent diary entries for this project (from any agent), and the top memories of the project. Prompt submit searches Palace with your actual question and injects matching memories before the agent answers (Claude Code and Codex). Post tool use recalls related memory while the agent greps and reads files, so earlier decisions surface without a search. Stop asks the agent to write a diary entry and record decisions if the session did real work but saved nothing. All hooks fail open: if the palace is missing or empty, the agent works as normal. Every result carries its wing, room, source file, drawer id and score breakdown, so you can see where an answer came from. Facts that change over time palace-rs has a temporal knowledge graph: subject → predicate → object, with a valid-from date. When a fact changes, the agent invalidates the old one and adds the new one, so the timeline keeps both. palace_conflicts flags facts that look stale or contradictory. Privacy claude-mem: "Anonymous usage analytics are on by default." Its telemetry page says it uses PostHog and calls it "on by default (opt-out)". You turn it off with npx claude-mem telemetry disable (or DO_NOT_TRACK ). The installer "asks you to sign in to claude-mem in your browser (email magic link)". Screenshots are "kept by default" under ~/.claude-mem/media-v1/ . palace-rs: No telemetry. palace gain statistics are written to your local database only. The only network calls are the one-time model download from Hugging Face and, if you turn it on, your own Palace Server in remote mode. No account, no sign-in, no analytics. Back up with palace export or by copying palace.db . Delete everything by removing ~/.palace . Side by side claude-mem 15.18.1 palace-rs 0.20.0 Language TypeScript Rust What you run Node + Bun + uv/Python + Chroma + HTTP worker One palace binary Storage SQLite + Chroma One SQLite file What's stored Observations and summaries written by an LLM observer (default: Claude Haiku) Your files, chats and notes, verbatim LLM / API key needed Yes (hosted observer, your key, or your Anthropic plan) No Published retrieval benchmark None in README LongMemEval R@5 0.987, no LLM Telemetry On by default (PostHog), opt-out None Account / sign-in at install Yes (email magic link) No License Apache-2.0 MIT GitHub stars 116,434 10 The point claude-mem is popular, and it covers a lot of agents. But popularity isn't architecture, and it isn't a benchmark. If you want memory that: is one binary you can audit, stores what happened rather than a model's summary of it, costs zero tokens to write, sends nothing anywhere, and comes with recall numbers you can reproduce, that's palace-rs, today. Don't trust the stars. Don't trust me either. Every quote above is from the projects' own pages. Open them and check. # macOS / Linux curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AncientiCe/palace-rs/main/scripts/install.sh | sh # Windows irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AncientiCe/palace-rs/main/scripts/install.ps1 | iex palace install Sources palace-rs README: https://github.com/AncientiCe/palace-rs claude-mem README: https://github.com/thedotmack/claude-mem claude-mem package.json (engines, version, license): https://github.com/thedotmack/claude-mem/blob/main/package.json claude-mem default settings: https://github.com/thedotmack/claude-mem/blob/main/src/shared/SettingsDefaultsManager.ts claude-mem telemetry doc: https://github.com/thedotmack/claude-mem/blob/main/docs/public/telemetry.mdx LongMemEval: https://github.com/xiaowu0162/LongMemEval Star counts and versions as of 2026-11-12.

title: It Worked Locally… But Did It Match Staging? Meet DiffLens
author: Praveen Kumar
summary: DiffLens: Compare Local and Staging Web Apps with Visual, Content, and Markup Diffs Have you ever finished a UI change, opened staging, and wondered: “What exactly changed between my local build and staging?” A manual check can miss small layout shifts, changed text, or unexpected DOM updates. I built DiffLens to make those differences easier to inspect. DiffLens is a local web app that compares a local page against a staging page in three independent ways: Visual diff: Which pixels changed? Content diff: Which visible text changed? Markup diff: Which elements or attributes changed? DiffLens — Compare. Understand. Ship with confidence. The problem: a screenshot does not tell the whole story A screenshot comparison is useful, but it only answers part of the question. A button may have moved by a few pixels. A heading may have changed. A link may look identical but point to a different URL. A DOM node may have been added without an obvious visual change. These are different kinds of changes, so DiffLens treats them as separate comparison layers. 1. Visual diff DiffLens captures both pages using Chromium at a fixed 1920 × 1080 viewport, then compares the screenshots using pixelmatch . Changed pixels are highlighted over a faded local screenshot. The UI provides side-by-side, slider-overlay, and diff-only views. The comparison summary also reports the percentage of pixels that differ. Treat this as a signal for investigation rather than a pass/fail score: dynamic content, font rendering, and page movement can all affect the result. 2. Content diff The content layer compares visible page text ( innerText ) line by line using the diff library. Adjacent delete/add pairs are presented as word-level modifications. Staging is the baseline; local is the candidate: Added: Content present in local but absent from staging. Removed: Content present in staging but absent from local. Edited: Existing content whose wording has changed. 3. Markup diff The markup layer compares element snapshots matched by rendered CSS path. It reports new nodes, removed nodes, text changes, and tracked attribute changes such as href , src , alt , aria-* , and form attributes. How it works Both URLs are loaded in parallel in isolated browser contexts, so cookies and browser storage are not shared between sides. Before capture, DiffLens blocks service workers, freezes animations and transitions, waits for fonts and images, and scrolls the page to trigger lazy-loaded content. It captures visible text, element snapshots, console/network diagnostics, and screenshots. The three diff layers then run and their results are assembled into a report. flowchart TD A[Local URL] --> C[Chromium capture] B[Staging URL] --> D[Chromium capture] C --> E[Local snapshot] D --> F[Staging snapshot] E --> G[Visual diff] F --> G E --> H[Content diff] F --> H E --> I[Markup diff] F --> I G --> J[Comparison result] H --> J I --> J J --> K[HTML report and JSON] Both pages use the same capture settings: Setting Value Viewport 1920 × 1080 Device scale factor 1 Locale en-US Colour scheme light Reduced motion Enabled Implementation notes DiffLens uses Chromium because visual comparison requires actual layout and paint. The Chromium build is installed for Playwright. pixelmatch powers screenshot comparison, while the diff library handles text comparison. Markup comparison uses captured element snapshots. Visual comparison The visual layer compares the two captured screenshots and identifies changed pixels. // Conceptual example of the visual comparison stage. const changedPixels = pixelmatch ( stagingImageData , localImageData , diffImageData , width , height , { threshold : pixelThreshold } ) ; Content comparison The content layer compares captured visible text, treating staging as the baseline and local as the candidate. // Conceptual example. const changes = diffLines ( stagingText , localText ) ; Markup comparison For markup, DiffLens captures each element's CSS path, tag, own text, and tracked attributes. The snapshots are matched by CSS path to identify additions, removals, and updates. These snippets illustrate the approach; they are not copied from the project's internal modules. Diagnostics and comparison details A visual or content difference is easier to investigate when you can also see how each page loaded. DiffLens includes a Diagnostics view with information for both sides, including HTTP status, page title, viewport, page height, visible text size, scanned element count, links/buttons/images, capture time, and console or request errors. More than a screenshot comparison Per-side headers and cookies Headers and cookies can be configured independently for local and staging. This is useful for pages behind authentication or feature flags. Basic Auth DiffLens supports preemptive Basic Auth on each side independently. Static comparisons pass credentials to Playwright through httpCredentials . Passwords are not persisted to localStorage , sent to the server, or included in exported artifacts. The UI stores only the username for display, and the password field is cleared after the session ends. Exportable results Each comparison produces a self-contained HTML report with embedded screenshots and a JSON result. Screenshots, text snapshots, and result.json are stored under .artifacts/<id>/ ; the latest 40 runs are retained. Try it locally Requirements Node.js 20+ macOS, Linux, or Windows Approximately 150 MB for the Chromium build Installation git clone https://github.com/praveen-pravi6B/difflens.git cd difflens npm install npm run setup:browser npm start Open http://127.0.0.1:4173 and select Try the demo . The bundled demo pages contain intentional differences so you can explore all three comparison layers. To compare your own pages, enter a local URL such as http://localhost:3000 and a staging URL such as https://staging.example.com . Select Compare pages , or use ⌘ + Enter on macOS / Ctrl + Enter on Windows and Linux. Useful commands npm start # Start the application npm run dev # Restart on file changes npm run setup:browser # Install Chromium npm run smoke # Run the end-to-end smoke test Limitations and security Dynamic content such as timestamps, A/B tests, live counters, and carousels can differ between captures. Full-page pixel diffs on long pages can be affected by vertical layout shifts. Canvas, WebGL, and video cannot be meaningfully compared as text or DOM. Bot protection may serve different content to headless Chromium. DiffLens fetches the URLs you provide, including internal hosts. It binds to 127.0.0.1 by default. Do not expose it to an untrusted network without adding authentication and appropriate SSRF protections. Only HTTP and HTTPS URLs are accepted. What's next? The next step for DiffLens is synchronized live rendering . Instead of comparing captured screenshots, this mode will render the local and staging pages side by side in the same workspace, so you can interact with both versions while reviewing them. The planned experience will include: Side-by-side view: see the local and staging pages next to each other. Slider view: use a draggable divider to reveal either page in a shared viewing area. Synchronized interactions: click a link or navigation item in one pane and the corresponding navigation action will happen in the other pane too. This makes it easier to follow the same user journey on both versions and compare the result as you go. This will build on DiffLens's existing comparison workflow by making it easier to inspect not only what changed in a capture, but also how both versions behave during the same interaction. If you work on frontend applications, QA, or UI testing, give it a try and let me know what would make it more useful.
